work.title: De Fuga Saeculi

paragraphs.text: We often talk about fleeing this world. If only our hearts were as wary and watchful as our talk is easy! What is worse, the lure of earthly desires often creeps in, and a flood of vanities takes hold of the mind, so that the very thing you are trying to avoid is what you think about and turn over in your mind. It is hard for a person to guard against this, and impossible to strip it off altogether. The prophet shows that this is something we pray for rather than something we achieve, when he says: “Incline my heart to your testimonies and not to covetousness.” For our heart and our thoughts are not in our power. They pour in unexpectedly and confuse the mind and soul, and drag them somewhere other than where you intended. They call us back to worldly things, plant earthly concerns in us, push pleasures on us and weave enticements around us. At the very moment when we are preparing to lift up our minds, empty thoughts break in, and usually we are thrown down to earthly things.

Who is so blessed that he always rises upward in his heart? And how can this happen without God's help? It cannot happen at all. So the same Scripture says above: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; ascents are in his heart.” Blessed indeed is the one whom pleasure does not call back and desire does not bend, who does not look back at lower things, which even Lot's wife could not escape. Warned by her example, the apostle forgot what lay behind and reached out for what lay ahead. He hurried toward the prize and was found worthy to reach it, because he saw Christ before him, who was calling him to the crown of righteousness. But he reached it because he denied himself in order to gain Christ. In the end it was not he who lived, but Christ lived in him.

Amid so many passions of this body and so many enticements of this world, who can keep his footsteps safe and undefiled? The eye looks around and turns the mind's attention away. The ear hears and bends its purpose. A scent is breathed in and hinders thought. The mouth tastes and brings back sin. Touch makes contact and kindles a fire. “Death has come in through the window,” said the prophet. Your window is your eye. If you look at a woman to desire her, death has come in. If you listen to a harlot's talk, death has come in. If luxury takes your senses captive, death has entered. So whoever wants to ascend should not pursue the joys of the world, nor what is pleasant and delightful, but what is full of sorrow and weeping. For “it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of rejoicing.” Indeed, Adam would not have gone down from paradise if he had not been deceived by pleasure.

So David, who had learned how dangerous even a person's glances can be, rightly calls blessed the one whose whole hope is in the name of God. For such a person does not look to vanities and follies, if he always fixes his attention on Christ and always looks on Christ with the inner eyes. That is why he again turns to him and says: “Turn away my eyes, so that they do not see vanity.” The circus is vanity, because it does no good. The speed of horses is vain, because it is a false hope of safety. The theater is vanity, and every game is vanity. “All is vanity,” said Ecclesiastes, all the things that are in this world. So whoever wants to be saved should rise above the world, seek the Word who is with God, flee this world and leave the earth behind. For he cannot grasp that which is and always is unless he first flees from here. That is why the Lord, intending to draw near to God the Father, said to the apostles: “Rise, let us go from here.”

The law too teaches you that the world must be fled and God followed. For what else does it teach when it says: “You shall set apart cities of refuge for yourselves, and they shall be refuges for you, to which the slayer may flee, anyone who has struck down a life unintentionally,” and further on: “You shall have six cities of refuge. You shall give three cities beyond the Jordan, and three cities you shall give in the land of Canaan”? Plainly these refuges were set up for those who flee there because of the crime of homicide, but let us look more deeply. There are four points that tell us the hidden meaning of this reading must be examined more profoundly. First, why were the six cities of refuge for those charged with homicide given from the cities that fell by lot to the Levites as their portion, and why were the cities of the other tribes not also assigned to this task? Second, why six in number? For this number does not seem to have been laid down idly, neither more cities nor fewer. Third, why were three of the cities that were to be a refuge for offenders placed beyond the Jordan and three in the region of Canaan? Fourth, why is a reckoning and limit of time included, during which the slayer is to live in the city of refuge until the high priest dies, and after the high priest's death the slayer is to return to the city where he lives? We must therefore speak about each point and settle these questions in the order in which we have set them out.

So we must first explain why it was fitting that the Levites' cities were given as refuges. Clearly it was suitably arranged, because the Levites are fugitives from this world. To please God they leave homeland, parents, children and all their kin, so as to cling to God alone. So too it was said to Abraham: “Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house.” But perhaps you will say: “He was not a Levite.” Yet he had Levi in his loins, as we read in the Letter to the Hebrews. And the Lord speaks to Levites when he speaks to his disciples, that is, the apostles: “If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.” And yet it has now been said to all: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for adoption.” The fullness has come; the remnant has ceased. For Christ has called everyone. The way out is open to all, so that all may follow; the kingdom and eternal life are set before all.

So the one whose portion is God should care for nothing but God, so that he is not hindered by the duty of some other need. For whatever is given to other duties is taken away from the worship of religion and from this office of ours. This is the true flight of the priest: renouncing his household and a kind of estrangement from those dearest to him, so that whoever longs to serve God denies himself to his own. So the decree of the eternal law rightly entrusted fugitives to fugitives, so that those who have forgotten this world might receive those who condemn their sins, seek forgetfulness of their former life and desire to wipe out the worldly deeds they have done. The minister of God's holy altar, then, is a fugitive from his own. That is why the Lord, as chief of priests, gave the Levites a pattern in his Gospel when he said: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” That is: I do not acknowledge a mother, I do not recognize brothers, I do not know my kin. “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” So the minister knows only the word of God, since he knows only those in whom the word of God is at work. And so he is an exile from the world. A fugitive from the body and from the passions, he renounces everything, so that he alone remains, as Elijah said: “And I alone am left.” But he was not alone, for Christ was with him. And the Lord himself was left alone, but he says: “I am not alone, for the Father is with me.” There is also this reason, that the Levites are ministers of God.

So their cities are assigned by the law to slayers in flight, because it is their right to carry out the divine commands with regard to those who have committed a deadly crime. The church does not know how to make its laws public; what it knows is that the priest must obey the Lord's command. Listen to a Levite saying: “I have handed such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Let the mind of the flesh in us, then, be struck by the Levite's sword and die, so that our soul may live. For unless the mind of the flesh is slain, there can be no fruit of eternal life.

The refuges of the six cities are these. The first city is the knowledge of the Word and a way of life shaped after his image. Whoever enters that knowledge is safe from punishment, as the Lord also says: “You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.” And elsewhere: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” So this city is like a mother city, and the other five cities of the Levites lie around it. The second city is the consideration of God's work, by which the world was created. The third city is the contemplation of royal power and eternal majesty. The fourth city is the beholding of God's mercy. The fifth city is the contemplation of the divine law that commands what must be done. The sixth city is the part of the law that lays down what must not be done. How great is the abundance of God's mercy, how great the riches of his kindness! He considered each person's pursuits and the frailties of the human condition, through which we are led into sin even against our will and resisting, and through which, overcome by enticements, we often commit faults we did not intend. So he set before us various refuges, namely six cities, so that by the same number in which the world was formed, a remedy might be provided against worldly vices and the shipwrecks of this age!

The first remedy, then, is this: if sin has crept upon a man of good purpose, and he wants perfect security, let him hurry without any delay to the very citadel of all things, where the Word of God is in the Father's bosom, that is, in God's secret and inner place, where the fountain of wisdom is. There, in place of death, he may drink the immortal draught of eternal life. The second remedy is for one who cannot taste beforehand the knowledge of that good and is slower either in mind or in grasping faith, since one reaches the heights of knowledge by the swift vigor of the mind and sharpness of intellect. Let him at least consider the Lord's works, and from the things that have been made let him contemplate the author of so great a work. For from the good things in the framework of this creation (for they are “very good,” as the Lord said) that supreme and eternal good is grasped. What order there is in things, what discipline, what grace! Is not even a slow mind moved by these to love its author? For if we love our parents because they begot us, how much more should we love the creator of our parents and our own maker! So the working power of God, though it is not seen, is nevertheless judged from its works, and his works reveal the worker, so that he who is not grasped may be understood. That is why the Lord says: “If you do not believe me, at least believe the works.” So this city too is a good refuge, since it bears witness to the grace of its builder and stirs our affection, so that we may long all the more for him who has evidently bestowed such beauty on us in this structure. The third rank is the contemplation of royal power, so that we submit to him as king if we do not defer to him as father. For often a man who is ungrateful for his salvation becomes obedient to authority out of fear of the one who presides, so that he who would not and could not recognize the grace of kindness recognizes the necessity of sober conduct. So necessity corrects the one whom kindness ought to have moved.

These are the three cities beyond the Jordan given as a refuge to the more perfect wisdom. The first is that we flee sin by training our mind to be conformed to the image of God. For so we were created, as God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” This, then, is the law of that first city. Next, if because of the frailty of the flesh and the enticements of the world we cannot shape our mind in this way, let us lighten our guilt by reverence for the Father who begot us and by the devotion of a child; for “love covers a multitude of sins.” So whoever could not be in the image of God, let him be in the fullness of love. The first city shuts sin out; this one releases it. This, then, is the law of the second city: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength.” But if there are again some so narrow and small of mind that they cannot receive the abundance and grace of love, you have the third city, so that dread of God's power may make you sober and fear may bend you. And this is the third law: “You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.” These, then, are the chief virtues, and so they belong to the few, not the many, and are placed beyond the Jordan: that you reproduce the archetype as its image, love him as a son loves his father, and worship him as a subject worships his king.

But those who have crossed the Jordan (and Jordan means “their descent”), that is, those who have come down from those higher virtues to these lower ones, in whom integrity, love and humility have wavered, have refuges closer to human nature to which they can go. So those who are guilty of offenses and bent by vices that were not willful may hope that the Lord can be reconciled to them if they ask for pardon. They may hope that they can be set right if they follow the commandments of the heavenly testaments, by which we are either shaped for innocence or called back from sin. These, then, are the cities that follow, on this side of the Jordan: that we make God favorable to us, follow what he commands and avoid what he forbids. So let there be eagerness to win God's favor, obedience in following his commands, and caution against transgressing his prohibitions. By these we may revere God's propitiating mercy and his lawgiving providence, either by obeying what he has laid down or by turning away from what he has forbidden.

There remains the fourth point, what is said about the death of the high priest: that the slayer will be in the city of refuge until that time, until the high priest dies. Here the literal interpretation gets stuck. First, the length of the refuge itself is fixed by chance rather than by the fairness of any judgment. Second, equal cases have unequal outcomes, for it could happen that the high priest died the day after that slayer took refuge. What kind of sentence is it that depends on something uncertain? So since the letter gets stuck, let us look for the spiritual meaning. Who is this high priest but the Son of God, the Word of God, whom we have as our advocate with the Father? He has no share in any sins, whether willful or accidental. In him all things on earth and in heaven hold together. For all things are bound by the bond of the Word and held together by his power, and they stand firm in him, since they were created in him and all fullness dwells in him. And so all things endure, because he does not allow what he has bound together to come apart, since they hold together by his will. For as long as he wills, he restrains and rules all things by his command and binds them in a natural harmony. So the Word of God lives, and lives above all in the souls of the devout, and the fullness of the Godhead never dies. For the everlasting Godhead and the eternal power of God never die. Yet he does die for us if he is separated from our soul. This is not because he is corrupted by death, but because our mind is loosed and stripped from union with him; for true death is the separation of the Word and the soul. Then at once the soul begins to lie open to willful sins.

We have these kinds of virtues not in outline but clearly expressed in the apostle, when he says: “So, for my part, I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. For I am not ashamed of the gospel; it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed,” that is, in the one who has believed. Then he added: “from faith to faith, as it is written: but the righteous lives by faith.” In whom, then, is the righteousness of God revealed, if not in the one who is conformed to the image of the Son of God? There you have the first precept, being in the image of God. The second: that the invisible things of God are understood through the things that have been made, that is, his eternal power and divinity are known through his works. This is the working power. The third concerns his imperial power, because the Word of God is royal and judicial and full of priestly justice. He keeps the reward of good deeds and the repayment of evil ones for those who will come to his judgment, about whom the apostle says: “We know that God's judgment falls according to truth on those who do such things.” So whoever has known the truth and justice of God should not do what deserves death. Next comes God's goodness, which is propitiatory, about which he says: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and forbearance, not knowing that God's goodness leads you to repentance?” That is, it ought to lead you. It calls you because God is good, so that you can hope for pardon of your sins; for he who is ready to forgive does not want to punish. He also added the giving of the law, that is, lawgiving, so that if anyone grows slack from contemplating God's goodness and is moved to carelessness rather than to repentance, he may follow the law, since, he says, “all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law.”

Now the law is twofold, natural and written: the natural in the heart, the written on tablets. So all are under law, namely the natural law, but it is not given to all that each should be a law to himself. That man is a law to himself who does of his own accord the things of the law and shows the work of the law written in his heart. You have the good things of the law, which we ought not only to know or hear in a perfunctory way but also to do; for “it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.” You have also learned what is evil. First of all, nature itself teaches good conduct. You know that one must not steal; and if your slave steals from you, you beat him, and if anyone makes advances to your wife, you think he should be prosecuted. So what you blame in others you commit yourself: “you who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” Then came the law, which was given through Moses, and “through the law comes knowledge of sin.” You have also learned what to turn away from, and yet you do what you know is forbidden. And what does the law accomplish, except that the whole world should be made subject to God? For it was not given only to the Hebrew; it also called the stranger, since it did not shut out the proselyte. But because the law could stop everyone's mouth but could not convert the mind, the final remedy of that last city was needed, in which there would be a saving refuge, so that the death of the chief of priests would free us from all fear of death and strip us of dread.

Who is he, if not the one of whom we read: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world”? God set him forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness. And understand that he is himself the great chief of priests. The Father swore concerning him, saying: “You are a priest forever.” Rightly “forever,” because all the others were temporary and under sin, but he has a priesthood that cannot pass away. All are under death, but he lives forever; for how could one who can save others perish himself? “For such a one,” he says, “was fitting for us.” The expression is correct, since among writers who took care in their choice of words and phrasing we find something similar, as when one says: “a higher place than was fitting for victors.” I have not passed over this so that we may know that the apostle uses natural words rather than common or artificial ones. “For such a chief,” he says, “was fitting for us, a priest who is righteous, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners and made higher than the heavens.” This, then, is the Word, who dwells above the heavens and enlightens all things. That is why we read that he was anointed by God the Father by nature, because the Word is the light that has enlightened every man coming into this world. This is the Word of God, in whom is the great priesthood, whose spiritual garments Moses describes in that vesture of the chief of priests. By his power he has clothed the world, and as if robed in it he shines in all things. He has also put on kinship with the human race by taking on this body, saying to the Lord … [?] and pouring out an unspeakable love, pouring himself into all by the Spirit and by the fullness of his Godhead, of whose fullness we have all received, so that we may know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge and be filled with all the fullness of God. For Christ is the head of all, from whom the whole body is brought forth and joined together by mutual connection, receiving its growth by building itself up in love. This, then, is the Word who is above all, who says to Moses in the building of that ark of the testimony: “And you shall put into the ark whatever testimonies I give you, and you shall make a covering, the propitiatory,” and further on: “You shall place the propitiatory on top of the ark, and you shall put in the testimonies that I will give, and I will make myself known to you from there and speak to you from above.” That is: from there, where I am above the heavens, where I am with the Father, from there I will speak to you.

So let us draw near to that throne of grace, supported by the help of faith and lifted up by its oars, fleeing this world and its contagion. And this is what fleeing means: to keep away from sins, to take on the form of the virtues after the likeness and image of God, to stretch our strength toward imitating God as far as our capacity allows. For the perfect man is the image and glory of God. That is why the Lord also says: "Be perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect." This, then, is to be like God: to have justice, to have wisdom, and to be perfect in virtue. For God is without sin, and so whoever flees sin is in the image of God. There is no doubt, then, that the one who keeps away from sin is fleeing. That is why the apostle also cries out: "Flee fornication." For the enticements of sins pursue us, lust pursues us; but you must flee it as you would a raging mistress who, if she catches you, will not let you rest by day or by night, but harries you, burns you, sets you on fire. Flee avarice, so that it does not seize you from within. Flee faithlessness, so that it does not entangle you in its nets. That is why the Lord also says: "When they persecute you in this city, flee to another. Truly I tell you, you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes." And indeed, although he seems to counsel flight because of the weakness of the flesh, the better flight belongs to the one who flees the enticement of the world, so that he is not held fast by anxiety over his riches, by gazing on his treasure, or by desire for this life, but with the mind's attention set straight he hastens to the glory of the heavenly kingdom, hurries toward the crown, and is not called back from the suffering of his body by looking at earthly things.

Flight, then, is a death, whether one actually undergone or one foreshadowed. And perhaps the lawful cities of refuge express this, so that we may flee to the heights of the virtues, which elsewhere he grants as rewards to the good investor, saying: "Because you were faithful in a little, you shall have authority over ten cities." The law knows six cities; but because the one who could say "I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it" fulfilled the law, he grants a more perfect number in reward.

So let us not be ashamed to flee; for this flight is glorious, to flee from the face of sin. So Jacob fled at his mother's urging; for Rebecca said: "Rise up and flee to Mesopotamia." So Moses too fled from the face of King Pharaoh, so that the royal court would not defile him nor its power ensnare him. Indeed, he reckoned the reproach of Christ more precious than the riches of Egypt. So David too fled from the face of King Saul and from the face of Absalom. And indeed, as he fled he grew in godliness: he spared the one who lay in wait for him and prayed for the safety of the parricide. So the Hebrew people fled, so that their faith and their life opened a way for them through the waves. That flight was the path of innocence, the road of virtue, the taking up of godliness. I dare to say that Jonah too fled to Tarshish in this way, not by a flight of the body but by an ascent of the mind, for he rose to the likeness of Christ, so as to become a type of Christ. "For as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights," he says, "so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights." For had he not fled in this way, he would never have been heard from the belly of the whale.

But if you doubt it, let Rebecca teach you how blessed was the flight that Jacob undertook. Rebecca urged him: "Flee," she said, "to Mesopotamia." And Isaac says: "Rise and go to Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel." In hymns or oracles, as has been written before us, Bethuel is called wisdom by many, while in Latin translation it means "daughter of God." So Jacob is sent into the house of wisdom and is told to take a wife from the daughters of Laban, who lived in Haran, which means "caves"; in them is a figure of the senses, which are, as it were, in the caves of the body: sight in the eyes, hearing in the ears, smell in the nostrils, taste in the mouth. For whoever delights in this world and dances in the pleasures of the body is subject to the passions of the senses and dwells and lodges among them. That is why Rebecca says that he should live with Laban a few days, not a long time, so that he would not be tinged by bodily pleasures and captured by the enticements of the world.

Yet she persuades him to live there so that, as one eager for learning, he might learn the powers of the senses and, as it were, certain places and regions of the flesh, so that he might know himself and come to know the violence of the flesh, what was created and for what purpose, and how each sense operates. "Whoever looks at a woman to desire her," he says. The eye looks wrongly in that way. Let the eye look, then, and perform its task, but let it not be steered toward a fall by the command of a slippery mind, so that it brings back vice in place of duty. A short time, then, is given for coming to know the senses, or rather for experiencing them, perhaps the first beginnings of tender youth, and at once he is called back, so that he does not totter too long on slippery ground and the inner footsteps of the soul are not submerged in the divided flood, so to speak, of this body and this world. And when he has either gained experience or has stood firm on unstable, uncertain and wet ground, he is called back by his mother, patience or perseverance, who says: "I will send to you and fetch you from there," so that even there, on slippery ground, you may find the safe harbour of wisdom, which will not let you toss about as in a shipwreck; and so that, having returned, you may know how to persevere in the worship of God and be in the assembly of the nations, signifying that by his faith the Church of the nations was to be gathered.

Instructed, then, in these disciplines of patience and perseverance, Jacob set out and gained for himself a union with wisdom, the partner of his purpose, with a rich dowry of prudence, with which he might pass the seasons of his life without any stumbling. With the treasure of wisdom added, he built up for himself a flock of varied sheep, but a rational flock, shining with the variety of many virtues. That is why he also cut back the boasting of his flesh, which is signified by the numbness of his thigh, without prejudice to the interpretation of the sacred mystery. By these virtues, then, as by steps, his mind ascended to heaven, and he came to know the secrets of God and was strengthened and filled, so that when Laban searched his house he found nothing empty with him, nothing vacant, no idols, no image of vanity. For with him there was not an image but the truth, not a likeness of sloth but the solid form of justice and the intelligible expression of living virtue. And so Laban searched his spiritual house and found no want [?]; for it was full, not of figures but of real things.

He could have found the foundations and heights of the virtues, had he not brought with him blindness of heart and the darkness of a faithless mind. Indeed, the Sodomites, their minds steeped in the blindness of wickedness, could by no means find the door of holy Lot. For how could an impious mind see either the going out or the coming in of a holy man? The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: "For the prince of this world is coming, and in me he finds nothing." How could he find nothing in him in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwelt, and dwelt bodily, from whom power went out and healed everyone? How could he find nothing in the solidity of virtue, in the abundance of wisdom, understanding and justice? You yourself said, Lord: "I am full"; you yourself said: "Put your hand into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing." The one who did not believe put in his hand and found you to be Lord and God. So it was not that you were empty, but that the prince of this world was blind and empty, who knows how to see only what is his own, knows how to find only what is his own, and does not know how to recognize the things that are Christ's.

Or, if it reads as many have it, "He finds nothing in me," this means: he will not find malice in me, because malice is nothing; he will not find a dead man, because he is not dead. For how will he find death in him who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they were? He will not find sin in me, he says, for I have taken away the sin of the world. For how does he have nothing who has all things, and, what is more, has all things that the Father has, as he himself says: "All things that the Father has are mine"?

Let us flee, then, from here, where there is nothing, where everything thought magnificent is empty, where even the one who thinks himself something is nothing and does not exist at all. "I saw the wicked man," he says, "exalted on high and lifted above the cedars of Lebanon, and I passed by, and behold, he was not." You too pass by as David did; pass by as the good servant, so that it may be said to you: "Pass along and recline at table." Pass by as Moses did, so that you may see the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and see the great sight. This is the great sight. But if you wish to see it, loose the sandals from your feet, loose every bond of iniquity, loose the chains of the world, leave behind the sandal, which is earthly. That is why Jesus sent out the apostles without sandals, gold and silver, or money, so that they would not carry earthly things with them. For whoever seeks the good is praised not for his sandals but for the swiftness and beauty of his feet, as Scripture says: "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace, who bring good news of good things!" So loose the sandals from your feet, so that they may be beautiful for bringing good news. He said "loose," not "bind." Loose them, so that you may pass by and find that the wicked man you used to admire on earth is nothing and can do nothing. Pass by, then; that is, flee from the earth, where there is malice, where there is avarice. That is why David says to you: "Turn away from evil and do good." To turn away is surely to flee; and evil is on earth, the good is in heaven. That is why he also added: "Seek peace and pursue it"; peace is in heaven. Indeed, coming from heaven he said: "Peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you." Therefore, since evils must be fled and avoided, and evils are on earth, and iniquities are on earth, let us flee earthly things, so that iniquities do not seize us. They seized even holy David, as he himself testifies, saying: "My iniquities have seized me, and I could not see," because the eye of the soul is blinded by the smoke of iniquity, so that it does not see the things that are bright. So, then, Laban could not see the good things of Jacob, nor the prince of the world the glory of Christ.

But perhaps you will say: Why, then, was Jacob sent to Laban, if Laban was blameworthy? If we consider the name, in Latin it means "white." So Jacob is told to go out toward brighter things. But because he was still carnal, we better understand this as the brighter things of this life. As one not yet perfect, he goes first to the man in whose light he might rejoice for a time. But Laban had worse sons, that is, his name was more tolerable than his deeds. And so, by his mother's counsel, by the divine oracle, and by the will of Jacob himself, a lover of discipline, Laban is deserted and left behind.

Rachel, however, hid the holy images, that is, the Church or prudence, because the Church knows nothing of empty ideas and the vain figures of idols, but knows the true substance of the Trinity. Indeed, she abolished the shadow and made manifest the brightness of glory. So let us leave the shadow, we who seek the sun; let us abandon the smoke, we who follow the light. Smoke is iniquity, because as smoke is to the eyes, so iniquity is to those who practise it. The shadow is life; for this life of ours on earth is a shadow, as Job said. And what is here but temptations? All time is spent in anxiety, all life in troubles. "You will walk in the midst of snares," he says. And another complained of snares stretched out but hidden for him on the way he walked. So as not to be caught and fall, he wanted to flee like a sparrow, but the snare was not yet broken. "Flight has perished from me," he says. His wings were weighed down by that dark water in the clouds of the air, and perhaps he could not fly. And so he sought to receive those wings, so that he might fly away and be at rest, as it is written: "Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest?" For where there is flight, there is rest. Indeed, elsewhere he says: "If you sleep among the lots, the wings of a dove covered with silver."

But perhaps you will say: How then does he say here that flight has perished from him, when earlier he had said: "If I take my wings before the dawn"? Is this a contradiction? Not at all. For many are the contests of the just. Does an athlete wrestle only once? How often, after many crowns, is he defeated in another contest! How often does one who has often won sometimes waver and hang in uncertainty! And often it happens [?] that a strong man engages with strong men and greater contests arise, where there are greater proofs of strength. So David, when he was seeking flight to escape his adversary, could not find his wings either. He was wavering in a contest whose outcome was in doubt, since where he has his wings in his power, the title of the psalm is "To the end," that is, to the perfection and completion of victory. Indeed, he says as a victor: "Lord, you have tested me and known me. You have known my sitting down and my rising up." Rightly did he have the ability to fly who had received the wings of resurrection; but here he is still in the cave, that is, in the flesh, in a kind of cavern of this body, contending with King Saul, the son of hardness, and with the power of that intelligible prince who is not seen but is understood. That is why the title of the psalm is "Of understanding"; David, though placed in the flesh, nonetheless brought it to a close, but he earned the bringing of it to a close by praying. Indeed, he begins with the voice of prayer.

Add to this that the one psalm is said to be spoken in the person of the Saviour, this one in the person of David, who did not have victory in his own power but hoped for it from Christ. And yet he too, after he stretched out his hands to God like the wings of his soul, took refuge in the Lord and asked for the guidance of the Holy Spirit, so that he might know the way by which he could ascend, saw the heavens bowed so that Christ might come down, and asked him to lift him up with his hand. Or perhaps he no longer sought his own wings because, having become more perfect, he longed for the hand of Christ.

Whoever, then, wishes to be lifted up by the hand of Christ, let him first fly upward himself; let him have his own wings — whoever flees the world has wings — and if he does not have his own — lest perhaps only he who has the power to fly has his own — if, I say, he does not have his own, let him receive them from him who has them. So whoever flees the world flies. "Behold," he says, "I went far off in flight and stayed in the wilderness." So David flew away like the night raven in its dwelling, like the solitary sparrow on the house. But if you apply it to Christ, he flew away in the suffering of his body, so as to protect the peoples of the nations under the shadow of his wings; he flew away in his divinity, he remained in his body and dwelt in the wilderness, so that the children of the desolate woman might be more than those of her who had a husband. Let us follow that body, then, so that we too may rise again; for where the body is, there the eagles will be also.

Whoever cannot fly like an eagle, let him flutter like a sparrow; whoever cannot fly to heaven, let him fly to the mountains; let him first flee the valleys, which are quickly corrupted by moisture, and cross over to the mountains. Abraham's nephew crossed over to the mountain of Zoar and was saved, but she who could not ascend, bending back with a woman's longing, lost her salvation. "Draw near to the everlasting mountains," the Lord says through the prophet Micah; "rise up from here, for this is no refreshment for you because of your filth. You have been corrupted with corruption; you have suffered persecution." And the Lord says: "Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains," where there is Mount Zion and Jerusalem, the city of peace, built not of earthly but of living stones, and ten thousands of angels, the church of the firstborn, the spirits of the perfect, the God of the just, who has spoken better in his blood than Abel. For Abel cried out for vengeance, he for forgiveness; Abel accused his brother's sin, he forgave the sin of the world; Abel exposed a crime, he covered it, according to what is written: "Blessed are those whose sins are covered."

But let whoever flees flee swiftly, so as not to be caught; let him swiftly plunder this world as the Hebrew plundered Egypt. Let her who is in labour give birth, so that she is not unable to flee with the womb of her mind burdened and weighed down with iniquities; and let her flee not as one carrying a nursing child but as one unencumbered, not bearing a little one but presenting one perfect in Christ. Let him flee not as one taking his holiday on the sabbath but as a labourer at his work, not as one barren in the cold but as one rich at harvest. That is why it was said: "Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath." So this flight is fruitful in virtues, not barren of merits. This flight knows nothing of the chill of fear, the trembling of death, the cramping of anxiety, the idleness of laxity, the holidays of wantonness, the torpor of sluggishness; rather it requires a tireless traveller toward the heavenly life, a vigorous candidate for the kingdom above, a wealthy farmer who gathers in his fruits and, in gathering them, seizes them eagerly.

For what else is asked of you, O man, but that you fear God, seek him, walk after him, and take hold of his ways? "With what," he says, "shall I take hold of the Lord? Shall I take hold of him with burnt offerings?" Not with ten thousand kids, not with thousands of rams, not with the fruits of impiety is the Lord reconciled and are sins redeemed; but the grace of the Lord is taken hold of by a good life. "It has been declared to you, O man," he says, "what is good. Or what else does the Lord require of you but that you do justice and love mercy and be ready to walk with the Lord your God?" So the Gospel says to you: "Rise, let us go from here"; the law says to you: "You shall walk after the Lord your God." You have learned how to flee from here: why do you delay? The Gospel says to you again: "Brood of vipers, who showed you to flee from the wrath to come?" And it says this to those who were coming to the baptism of repentance.

So repentance is a good flight; the grace of God, in which the one who flees is taken up, is a good flight; the wilderness is a good flight, to which Elijah, Elisha and John the Baptist fled. Elijah fled the woman Jezebel, that is, the outpouring of vanity, and fled to Mount Horeb, which means "drying up," so that the carnal flood of vanity might be dried up in him and he might know God more fully. For he was at the brook Cherith, which means "knowledge," where he might drink in the flowing abundance of divine knowledge, fleeing the world in such a way that he did not even seek food for this body except what the birds brought him as servants, although his food was for the most part not earthly. Indeed, he walked forty days in the strength of the food he had received. Surely so great a prophet was not fleeing a woman but this world; nor did he fear death, he who had offered himself to the one who sought him and who said to the Lord, "Take my soul," enduring weariness of this life, not desire for it. Rather he was fleeing the enticement of the world, the contagion of a stained way of life, and the sacrileges of an impious and transgressing nation.

Solomon too, under the figure of that woman, sets forth the corruption of this world and teaches that the arts of the harlot are to be avoided. This is the strange woman, the fornicator, from whom he urges you to guard yourself and not to turn your heart aside to the ways of the world, but to place it in the hand of the Lord, in which is the heart of the king. For whoever rules himself, which is worth more than commanding others, has his heart in the hand of God, and God turns it wherever he wishes. It is no wonder that he turns it to good, he who is of perfect goodness. Let us be in the hand of God, then, so that we may seek the good, that incorruptible and unchangeable good of which the prophet Amos says: "Seek good and not evil, that you may live; and so the Lord God Almighty will be with you, as you have said: We have hated evil and loved good." So where God who is good is, there are the good things which David longed to see and believed he would see, as he himself says: "I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living." For those are good things which remain forever, which cannot be corrupted by the change of time or age.

Whoever has sought God and found him is among those good things. For where a man's heart is, there is his treasure also; for the Lord is not accustomed to deny the gift of good to those who pray to him. Therefore, since the Lord is good, and is especially good to those who wait for him, let us cling to him, let us be with him with all our soul, with all our heart, with all our strength, so that we may be in his light and see his glory and enjoy the grace of heavenly delight. Let us lift up our minds, then, to that good, and let us be in it and live in it and cling to it, the good which is above every mind and every reflection and enjoys perpetual peace and tranquillity; and peace is above every mind and above every sense. This is the good which penetrates all things, and we all live in it and depend on it, while it has nothing above itself, but is divine; for no one is good but God alone. So what is good is divine, and what is divine is good. And so it is said: "When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness"; for by the goodness of God all good things are rightly bestowed on us, good things with which no evil is mixed. These good things Scripture promises to the faithful, saying: "You shall eat the good things of the land." Let us therefore be like that good, so that we may obtain the things that are good, the good that is without iniquity and without deceit and without harshness, with grace, with godliness, with sincerity and kindness, love and justice. And so goodness embraces all the virtues like a fruitful mother.

There is, then, no small reason why we ought to flee from here: so that we may pass from evils to good things, from what is uncertain to what is trustworthy and full of truth, from death to life. The Lord himself, by saying, "I have set before you good and evil, life and death," showed that life is the good, but eternal life. For if this life is subject to the world and its wickedness, then surely that life is good which is not corrupted or changed, which does not degenerate through any vice, and which is gained by virtue. Let us flee, then, the wickedness of this world, in which, he says, "the days themselves are evil," and let us flee without delay. And so Isaiah cries out: "Be strong, you slack hands and loosened knees." That is, be strong, you knees not of the body but of the soul, so that the mind's step, set straight, may be lifted to the highest heights of heaven, and its course may be firmer, its life more mature, its grace fuller, its prudence more watchful.

For this is what it means to flee: to know where you are heading, to raise yourself up from the world and from the body. Otherwise someone may again exalt himself in vain, and people puffed up in the mind of their flesh may fail to hold fast to the Head, so that it is said of them: "They fled and did not see." Rather, to flee from here is to die to the elements of this world, to hide one's life in God, to turn aside from corruptions, not to touch desires, and not to know the things of this world. The world lays all kinds of sorrows upon us. When it has filled us it empties us, and when it has emptied us it fills us. And all these things are empty and void, and there is no solid fruit in them. The rich man died and has nothing, because he is not rich toward God. He is therefore a fool, since wisdom is the worship of God, and to keep away from evil is discipline.

Who, then, would not flee the place of wickedness, the workshop of depravity, a wickedness that does not know how to die? It was not for nothing that a sign was set upon Cain so that no one would kill him. This signified that wickedness is not extinguished or removed from the earth. Cain was afraid of being killed because he did not know how to flee. For wickedness grows and piles up through its very practice. It has no measure and no end, and it fights with deceit and fraud. It is betrayed by its own deeds and by the blood of those it has slain, just as Cain too was betrayed. So wickedness dwells on the earth and wanders about here. That is why we pray that God's will may be done on earth as it is in heaven, so that innocence may be here too. Since wickedness has no place there, it prowls here, rages here and pours itself out. It was not drowned by the flood that covered the world, nor burned up by the fire of Sodom. In fact, it later sprouted more vigorously from its seedbeds, until it laid parricidal and sacrilegious hands on the very Author of salvation for all. The law condemns the deed, but it does not take away wickedness. The Lord Jesus himself condemned sin but put off the punishment of its author, so that there might be someone by whom the righteous are tested. For since God did not make evil, and it was the devil's wickedness that planted it, God postponed vengeance so that the devil might be conquered by the very people he had deceived.

So those who were deceived are put through training. In this way they pay the price of their credulity and take up the pursuit of virtue and a careful watchfulness. That is why he says: "Be wise as serpents." Why as serpents? So that the serpent may in turn be stripped of what is his, and he who wanted to strip others may lose what belongs to him. I do not mean his poisons, but the merits of his nature. In fact, he is cast down when you have ascended. For it is written: "I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven." He does not say "lightning" but "like lightning," because Satan lost the light he had before he tried to take your light from you. But perhaps you will point to what we read about the Savior: "As the lightning flashes from beneath heaven, so will the coming of the Son of Man be." Here too "like lightning" is right, because he is above lightning. After all, lightning comes from beneath heaven, but the true light is above heaven. So Satan is like lightning because he lost what he had, but you have received back what you had lost.

For the sentence has not been lifted from him as it has from you. The grace of Christ, which set you free, bound him fast, and the curse directed against the serpent because of your deception remains. For this is what was said to him: "Cursed are you above all the cattle of the earth." He who was the foe of good things is the common enemy of all, and he is condemned on behalf of those he had not yet harmed. For he who harmed man, to whom all those creatures are subject, harmed them all. He broke the common law, since he himself is subject to man along with the rest. That is why his curse is weighed down with the common hatred and loathing of all. The kind of condemnation, however, is not death but long-lasting punishment. "Upon your breast and belly," he says, "you shall go." For the guilty conscience had to be pressed down, wickedness had to be trampled, and the treacherous secret had to be banished, as it were, from the face of God. At the same time it is shown that the wickedness that bends one down to the earth is earthly. Then he added: "And you shall eat earth all the days of your life."

These words do seem to describe the nature of the serpent, but much more do they describe every vessel of wickedness, every serpent of depravity. Such a one throws itself onto its belly, shuts its poison up inside itself and rolls it about within its breast. It is slippery in its thoughts and walks upon its own frauds. It entangles itself in its own tricks. As it thinks, it is always stirring and churning its poisons, and it also crushes its belly, that is, the seedbed of its heart. That is why David puts it so well: "Sinners are estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken lies. Their fury is like that of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of the charmers and of the sorcerer, which are charmed by the wise." For this reason, too, the saying we read in the prophetic book seems well put: "My belly, I grieve for my belly." For wickedness is there where innocence ought to be. The part that ought to be calmest in us toils the hardest. It is trampled by the footprints of wickedness, goaded by claws, and shaken by the steady advance and growth of depravity, there where the generative seed of eternal posterity lies. This does seem to refer to his grief that the sons he had begotten and raised had perished, but much more to his grief that he did not have the seedbed of the Word in his belly. So he says "my belly" as of something most precious. For the womb of the mind is precious. In it a fruitful crop of counsels usually springs up from the seed of the Word, and in it the limbs, so to speak, of one's whole life, of the virtues and of disciplines, are usually formed.

But let us return to our subject, which is that God thought wickedness should be held in check for the time being rather than abolished. He says to the serpent: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and the woman's seed. She will watch for your head, and you for her heel." Where there is enmity, there is discord and the desire to harm, and where there is the desire to harm, there wickedness is set. So there is discord between the serpent and the woman. Wickedness lies beneath discord, and so wickedness has not been removed. Indeed, the serpent was left the task of watching for the heel of the woman and of her seed, in order to harm it and pour in its poison. So let us not walk on earthly things, and the serpent will not be able to harm us. Let us put on the shoe of the gospel, which shuts out the serpent's poison and blunts its bite, so that our feet may be shod for the gospel. Perhaps that is why Moses is told to loose the shoe from his feet: so that he might put on the shoe of the gospel. Or perhaps it is because the preaching of the gospel belonged not to Moses, that is, not to the prophets, but to the apostles. That, as we said above, is the sentence pronounced against the serpent. Let us now consider what kind of sentence was directed against man.

He who is the author of the sin is cursed, but the one deceived by another's fraud is not cursed. Yet because he did not keep God's commandment, he is condemned to toil at his work. The earth is indeed cursed, but in the works of the sinner, and he is cursed until he dissolves into earth. That is why Jesus took on flesh: to abolish the curse of sinful flesh. He was made a curse for us, so that blessing might swallow up the curse, purity swallow up sin, pardon the sentence, and life death. He also took on death, so that the sentence might be fulfilled and the judgment satisfied: sinful flesh was cursed until death. So nothing was done against God's sentence, since the terms of the divine sentence were fulfilled. The curse lasted until death; after death comes grace. We are dead, then, to the world. Why do we still make decisions about the world? We have died with Christ. Why do we still go after the business of this life? We carry the death of Christ about in our body, so that the life of Christ may also be revealed in us. So we no longer live that life of ours but the life of Christ: a life of innocence, a life of chastity, a life of simplicity and of every virtue. We have risen with Christ. Let us live in him and ascend in him, so that the serpent cannot find a heel of ours on earth to wound.

Let us flee from here. You can flee in spirit even if you are held back in body. You can be here and also be present with the Lord, if your soul clings to him, if you walk after him in your thoughts, if you follow his ways by faith and not by sight, and if you take refuge in him. For he is a refuge and a strength, and David says to him: "I fled to you and was not deceived." Since God is a refuge, and God is in heaven and above the heavens, we must surely flee from here to there, where there is peace and rest from labor, where we may feast on the great sabbath. As Moses said: "And the sabbaths of the land shall be food for you." For to rest in God and to see his delight is a banquet full of joy and peace. Shall we who have taken refuge in God go back to the world, then? Shall we who have died to sin go after sins again? Shall we who have renounced the world and its ways stick fast once more in its mud? Let us flee from here, for the time is short.

Listen to how you are to flee: "Let those who have wives be as though they had none, those who weep as though they were not weeping, those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, those who buy as though they did not own anything, and those who use this world as though they did not use it, for the form of this world is passing away." So let our works not pass away with the passing form of the world, or we too may pass away. Let us rather abide in the truth. If we abide in Christ, we abide in the truth. We shall abide with him and shall not pass away, but we shall say: "The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we bless you in the name of the Lord." Those who pass by cannot say this, for, as the prophet said, "Those who passed by on the way did not say, 'The blessing of the Lord be upon you.'" So if we want our works not to pass away, let us not pass by God's commandment. Let us not pass by the care we owe to seeking the Lord Jesus and earning his grace. That woman did not pass him by. She went right into the house of the Pharisee where Christ was reclining at table and poured ointment over his feet.

Let us not pass by the chance to make progress in any discipline, just as the young Joseph did not pass it by. He was looking for his brothers and hurried to the place where they were grazing the sheep, and when he learned that they were in Dothan, he went there. The word Dothan signifies a fitting failing, that is, a failing of vain opinions. It is no moderate failing but a complete and full one, and in it lies the soul's progress. For the wise man gains when he loses, since worldly opinions, which are compared to weak women, fail. That is why, to show that Sarah had reached the point of progress where she could bring forth laughter and joy, Scripture puts it so well: "It had ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women." So the failing of desires is good, and the failing of vanity is good, because it means that truth is added. That is why the saint also says: "My soul has failed for your salvation." For Sarah was about to bear the one whom God had granted and therefore had also promised. She was about to bring forth joy and that sober intoxication of gladness. Pregnant with wisdom, she was about to give birth through the quickness of her natural ability, before the expected time of delivery. You also read of the other Hebrew women that they give birth before the midwives arrive. This is because the souls of the righteous do not wait for arts and disciplines to arrive at their discoveries, nor do they need help in giving birth. Of their own accord they bring forth their offspring and come before anyone expects it.

Jacob was just as quick to find as he was to carry out. When his mother told him to bring food to his father, we see that he had the different kinds of definitions ready at hand. For he found quickly and also testified that God was the author of what he had found. This signifies both the prize of diligence and the richness of natural ability. The first definition, then, concerns discovery. What is found is sought; what is sought takes time; and what takes time certainly belongs to diligence. But what comes before any use of time is poured in by God and given by God, and what God gives belongs to nature, not to diligence. Natural ability, then, is a divine gift, and what is a divine gift belongs to nature. So ability belongs to nature and discovery to diligence. The one is without time, while the other needs time. The one is ready in an instant, while the other is searched out over a span of time. The one is above us, while the other is credited to us.

His father, then, was asking for the food of the word, for man does not live by bread alone but by every word of God. Isaac was asking for this kind of food, and Peter hungered for this kind of food when he saw the mysteries of the Gentile people who were going to believe. But Esau did not have at hand the food of a spiritual and quicker ability. While he hunted and searched and got ready to offer some very hard and rustic speech, Jacob got there first by quick discovery. With a gentle and almost homely reply he served up a sweet word to soothe and delight his father. So his father was amazed and said: "What is this that you found so quickly, my son?" Jacob answered: "What the Lord your God delivered into my hands." The first definition is in the question, the second in the answer. So the father found everything complete that belonged either to ability or to diligence, and he summed it up with a crowning definition, saying: "See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field that the Lord has blessed." For a field has both a natural ability to be fertile and the diligence of cultivation over time, and fullness rightly belongs to a field that lacks neither. At the same time, by adding "that the Lord has blessed," he seems to have ranked the grace of nature above the labor of cultivation. And Esau confirmed it, saying: "Rightly was he named Jacob, for he has supplanted me twice now and taken my birthright."

But perhaps you will ask: Why was the one his father sent to hunt delayed? Consider, though, that the father himself declared that Esau could not have ready what was being asked for in a spiritual sense. So, since Esau lacked natural ability, his father required him to add the help of diligence. He also urged him to hurry, saying: "Take your bow and arrow." Yet whoever acknowledges that the gift of natural ability is higher also receives the fruit of diligence.

It was right that Jacob brought homely food, since from the home store of his own seed he had gained union with wisdom. Diligence is good when joined to wisdom, and discovery is good when joined to natural ability. Indeed, holy Isaac, who had union with wisdom close at hand, walked in the field, or rather was carried out of himself. Let us too first be joined to wisdom, and then go out into the field eager to seek and to find. For many people seek badly, without wisdom. Cain, because he had not received prudence from God, sought badly and went out into the field badly. Abel went out well, for he offered a perfect sacrifice. Wisdom is a good sacrifice, and faith and every virtue are a good offering. Indeed, Wisdom has slaughtered her victims and mixed her wine in her bowl. So to give the drink of faith to the foolish Gentiles, she called them to her bowl, saying: "Whoever is foolish, let him turn aside to me." And to those lacking understanding she said: "Come, eat of my bread and drink the wine I have mixed for you." Plato thought he should carry this bowl over into his own books, and he called souls to drink from it. But he did not know how to satisfy them, because the drink he served was not faith but faithlessness.
Let us flee from here, then, as holy Jacob fled from his homeland, for he knew that the true homeland is the one above.

Let us flee as the deer flee to springs of water. Let our soul thirst for what David thirsted for. What is that spring? Hear him say: “For with you is the spring of life.” Let my soul say to this spring: “When shall I come and appear before your face?” For the spring is God. But whoever longs for this spring must pour out his soul upon himself, so that he leaves nothing in the possession of the flesh, but his soul overflows everywhere.

Susanna poured out her soul beautifully, so that the fires of the body, the terrors of death and the desires of this life could not rise up into it. Her soul, poured out upon her, put out every desire of the flesh and every worldly pursuit. It could even have quenched the flames of those monstrous old men and shameless elders, had not a flood of lust overflowed in them. When they threatened her with a false charge if she refused to consent to adultery, Susanna groaned and said: “I am hemmed in on every side. For if I do this, I shall perish by eternal death; but if not, I shall not escape your hands.” Yet she judged it better to flee the sin than the danger. So she wept when the crime was laid against her; she wept when they claimed for themselves the right to judge a modest and chaste woman as an adulteress. She did not lament death; she wept for the slander against her chastity and the wrong done to her faith. And she poured out upon herself not her body but her soul; for she would have poured out her body had she given in to the desires of the flesh. Then, when she was condemned to death, she cried out as though she were the judge of the guilty and the arbiter of her slanderers, and with the authority of an innocent conscience she summoned God's own inquiry into her case, not stirred by fear of death but raised high by the power of a judgment that convicts. So Susanna fled the world and entrusted herself to God, fleeing to that citadel of the eternal city which embraces the whole world, since all things are within God.

Paul too fled, let down through a window in a basket to make his escape (for he knew that a threefold cord cannot be broken). But he fled in order to preach the gospel of the Lord throughout the whole world, and so he was caught up into paradise. Let us also flee through the window, hearing the Lord's commandments and keeping them with sober sight and chaste eyes.

Let us flee like Lot, fearing the crimes of Sodom more than its punishments. For surely it is the more devout man who flees the contagion of wickedness: he shut his house against the Sodomites; though he lived among them he did not know them, for he knew nothing of their shameful deeds and turned away from their disgraceful acts; and as he fled he did not look back at those whose way of life he had no desire for. So he flees as Lot did who renounces vices, who disowns the ways of those he lives among, who does not look behind him, who enters that city above by the gateway of his thoughts and does not leave it until the high priest dies, he who took away the sin of the world. He died once for all, indeed, but he dies for each one who is baptized into the death of Christ, so that we may be buried with him and rise again with him and walk in the newness of his life.

You flee well if your heart does not imitate the counsels and thoughts of sinners. You flee well if your eye shuns cups and bowls, so that it does not grow bloodshot while it lingers over wine. You flee well if your eye turns away from another man's wife, so that your tongue may guard the truth. You flee well if you do not answer a fool according to his folly. You flee well if you take the steps of your feet away from the mouth of the foolish. For with bad guides one quickly goes astray; but if you want to flee well, keep your ways far from their words.

The high priest has died for you; he was crucified for you, so that you might cling to his nails. For in that flesh he took up both you and your sins; the bonds of your debts were nailed to his gibbet, so that you now owe nothing to the world, which you renounced once for all. And rightly you owe it nothing, if you are able to say: “For the world is crucified to me, and I to the world”; so that now you need not fear death, if you bear Christ, in whom you can say: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” For when that old self of ours was nailed to the cross, sin was destroyed, its sting blunted, guilt made void, so that we might no longer be slaves to shameful deeds. For the old self has passed away. Now there is no longer the old self in us, but a new creation bearing in itself the likeness of Christ: buried with him in the likeness of his death, we have taken on the image of his life and received the wings of spiritual grace.

So fly, then, in such a way that it may be said of you: “Who are these that fly like a cloud, and like doves with their young?” so that your clouds may rain down righteousness and your doves bring forth simplicity. Sail as men crossing over the world, not wandering about like the ships of Tarshish, so that you may set your course for the harbours of the mind and bring home the riches of the sea. Make such haste that it may be said of you: “They were swifter than eagles.” For you see that we must flee from the wrath to come, which those will be able to escape who through repentance have laid up for themselves a hope of escape and have drawn faith in the reconciliation to come, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belongs the kingdom from the ages, both now and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.
